magnetic_diversion.rule: A pre-energized, elongated axial/cusp-like field zone around and behind the Lance diverts charged or ionized debris plasma (Q4). It must exist before impact; neutral dust is not assumed to respond and needs physical interception.

diversion_boundary.rule: Magnetic field assists only charged or ionized particles; neutral dust is not assumed to curve around the ship.

regenerative.rule: Segmented Brow laminate with self-sealing/microvascular repair layers, serviceable rear structure and replaceable panels behind sacrificial full-area disruptor layers. Healing repairs survivable damage; it does not erase impact energy.

repair_escalation.rule: Automatic microrepair, then feedstock- and time-limited local patch, then external crawler, drone or crew panel replacement for major loss.

crown.rule: Concealed annular close-in defence around the Brow rim: twelve protected bays at 30 degrees behind the shield rim; threat-facing sectors translate mainly forward within the ~90 m projected Brow silhouette. Active mitigation, not primary armour and not a substitute for avoidance.

crown_engagement.rule: Local pulsed ablation/ionization for tracked small threats. Sacrificial canisters/pellets are primarily deployed early to seed a forward Dustbreak Veil, not fired as last-millisecond interceptors; fragmentation close to the ship is disfavoured and large objects stay avoid/deflect/ablate problems.

crown_concealment.rule: Weapons stay recessed behind the shield rim under armoured shutters or protected bays in normal flight; normal engaged hardware stays inside the r ~45 m projected Brow silhouette and translates mainly forward, and up to four threat-facing sectors may cooperate while the rest stay protected (14!C20, Eye 40!A27).

fiji_assistance.rule: The Fiji lattice may serve secondarily to shape or lighten the proactive diversion field; conventional electrical systems establish and store the field energy.

diversion_field.reason: Field strength, coil geometry, topology, power and ionization method are OPEN (OD-018). The 1 T over 10,000 m3 study point is DIAGNOSTIC and the displayed field lines are a PROTOTYPE visualization only.

repair.reason: Repair rate, feedstock and reservoir mass and maximum recoverable damage are OPEN (OD-019). damage_state and repair_state are normalized display controls only.

crown.reason: Ring radius, carriage count and travel, bay and shutter geometry, effector mix, engagement envelope, mass and power performance are OPEN (OD-021). The physical Crown here is the PROTOTYPE proxy in forward_shield.prototype.

crown_effective_aperture.reason: No single 90 m effective aperture is canonical (Q7). The 90 m D_crown_eff (Eye 02!A22, DIAGNOSTIC, phasing OPEN) is a theoretical whole-ring upper bound, not the Crown radius; the PROTOTYPE housing is not fitted to it.

preset_status.rationale: HIGH_POWER and FIRST_IGNITION show HIGH_POWER_REJECTION (07!A36, 40!A35 and 11!E4: full thermal duty). COAST (residual drive and lattice heat at low load), LOW_THRUST (the actual reduced load) and EVA (a throttled safe low output) show HEAT_ADMITTED (Q41, 40!A69, 11!E2:E5): the loads are unquantified (radiators.drive_waste_heat and the EVA throttle are OPEN), so no partial intensity is invented. DOCKED shows COOLANT_FLOW: the drive is off, but the loop keeps circulating while equipment is warm or hot and stops only once it is safe (11!G6, 40!A69); the stop is not shown. POST_SHUTDOWN_COOLDOWN is reachable through the control and the timeline. No preset isolates a cell. The coolant state of each configuration is radiators.coolant_modes, independent of thrust.

fault_pattern.rationale: A deterministic scatter (rank = global cell index x stride mod N, stride coprime with N) so isolated cells read as distributed local damage across all three blades and both zones. No damage distribution is sourced (OD-010 OPEN); any stride coprime with N is acceptable. Repair and requalification follow the same order, so a requalified cell was resurfaced and a resurfaced cell was isolated.

WF_RING_STOP_LOCK.description: Stop and lock before high thrust: motor-braked regenerative spin-down while levitated, stop at the index angle, index lock, set down on the touchdown cartridges at zero speed, then the ring-stop locks. The rings stay full size and no room turns.

WF_ROTOR_TOUCHDOWN.description: Loss of levitation on rotor 1 (example): it lands on its touchdown cartridges at speed and brakes to a stop; rotor 2 stays levitated and brakes on the same curve. Inspection required before full-speed service.

WF_VESTIBULE_SEAL_FAULT.description: A leak path across a vestibule seal on rotor 1 (example): the hatches isolate the vestibule, the health alarm and inspection flags are raised and both rotors stop and lock on the stop-lock curve (matched spin-down keeps the counter-rotating momenta cancelled). The second seal plane still holds the pressure boundary.

canon.architecture: Stationary pressure trunk -> independently closable stationary-side hatch -> double-boundary despun/spin-transfer vestibule per ring (an isolated intermediate volume that synchronizes between the stationary and ring motion) -> independently closable rotating-side hatch at each crew spoke/tube -> pressurized spoke -> occupied sector (Q46, 12!C11). Electrical/data transfer plus only essential rotary fluid interfaces. The rotary seal is never the sole pressure boundary.
canon.refuge_rule: One concentrated stationary refuge rated for 12 adjacent to the stationary transfer-hub region; reachable with rings rotating or stopped (I4).

hotspots.title: Despun transfer vestibule
hotspots.what: An isolated drum between the stationary spine and ring A. It holds still with the spine, or turns with the ring, so a crew member never steps across a moving edge.
hotspots.why: The ring turns at its working rate while the spine does not. Grabbing a spinning wall, or one seal carrying the pressure alone, is unsafe; two independently closable boundaries and a drum that matches speed first remove both risks.
hotspots.show: The map isolates the spine, the drum and ring A, cuts the hull away and marks the spine port gate and the drum door with their live state.

facts.label: Drum size, seals, sync cycle time
facts.reason: MEC-019 fixes the architecture (two independently closable boundaries around an isolated transfer volume that synchronizes with the ring); drum size, seals, bearings, hatch actuation and cycle time stay OPEN (16!I20, 12!G11).

hotspots.title: Storm refuge
hotspots.what: One shielded shelter for the whole crew in the stationary spine, beside the transfer hub. It does not turn, so it is reachable whether the rings spin or stand still.
hotspots.why: A solar storm leaves too little time to shield every room. Concentrating mass around one shelter close to the transfer path protects everyone at a fraction of the mass, and a stationary room never waits for a ring to stop.
hotspots.show: The map isolates the stationary spine with the transfer drums beside it.

facts.label: Structure and material stack

hotspots.title: Garden and life support
hotspots.what: Plant racks and the life-support bays share the common sectors of each habitat ring, under the ring's own gravity.
hotspots.why: Plants and water handling work best with a floor and a settled liquid surface. Mirroring the same functions in both rings means losing one ring does not lose the Garden or the air loop.
hotspots.show: The map isolates habitat ring A; the common sectors hold the Garden.

hotspots.title: Radiator blades
hotspots.what: Long fixed blades that run fore and aft along the flight axis and glow away the drive's waste heat into space.
hotspots.why: In vacuum heat leaves only as radiation, so the surface must be large and hot. Blades edge-on to the flight axis stay inside the forward shield's shadow and outside the plume.
hotspots.show: The map isolates the radiator blades from the hull.

facts.label: Mechanism
facts.value: Fixed blades; no fold/deploy mechanism (R1/R8, MEC-012)

hotspots.title: Drive and nozzles
hotspots.what: The fusion drive at the stern: one core feeding a common region, a manifold and the nozzles.
hotspots.why: Everything else on the ship is arranged around this line of thrust: the radiators, rings and shield keep clear of its plume and field.
hotspots.show: The map isolates the drive and its nozzles.

facts.label: Exclusion rule
facts.value: Radiator surfaces and coolant trunks remain outside nozzle plume and strong-field exclusion zones.

hotspots.title: Forward shield and EYE
hotspots.what: A broad shield at the bow, with the EYE sensor facets recessed in wells in its face, watching the path ahead.
hotspots.why: At speed, anything ahead of the ship arrives from the front. The occupied rings and the radiators stay inside the shield's silhouette, and the EYE looks out from behind the shield face instead of from an exposed nose.
hotspots.show: The map isolates the shield and the EYE at the bow and opens the forward defense explorer: observe the Eye placements and the Crown bays, replay an unresolved-dust case, inspect damage and repair. Remote view only.

facts.label: Shadow rule
facts.value: At nominal high-speed attitude, occupied rings and vulnerable radiator surfaces remain inside the projected forward-shield silhouette.

facts.label: Field of view
facts.reason: Broad forward cone; no degree value is locked. A rig may visualize a nonbinding cone.

hotspots.title: Maintenance drones
hotspots.what: Task-specific service robots: survey flyers, ring rovers and duct crawlers inside; Brow, radiator-root, spine and aft crawlers outside; two fixed arms. Each has its own dock, and none is a universal robot.
hotspots.why: Six people cannot inspect the whole ship by EVA. Docked robots on fixed tracks can survey and fetch, but only where a released safe state allows. They never cross the moving rings or the hot blades, never work on the ram face, and they are tools under crew and Seraph supervision, not persons.
hotspots.show: The map marks every proposed dock and arm base and opens the spine crawler demonstration: a service run along its track and three fault replays. Simulation only; every performance value is OPEN.

bodies.name: Sun
bodies.why: Every orbit on this chart is drawn around it. Wayfarer's distance from it at any moment is not released, so the chart cannot say how far away the ship is.

bodies.name: Mercury
bodies.why: The most eccentric planetary orbit: its distance from the Sun changes by about half between perihelion and aphelion, so one orbit guide circle hides a wide band.
bodies.derived: a_au, perihelion_au, aphelion_au = 10^6 km x 1e6 / au_km (IAU 2012 B2); radius_km = diameter_km / 2

bodies.name: Venus
bodies.why: The most nearly circular orbit of the planets: here the guide circle and the real path almost coincide.
bodies.derived: a_au, perihelion_au, aphelion_au = 10^6 km x 1e6 / au_km (IAU 2012 B2); radius_km = diameter_km / 2

bodies.name: Earth
bodies.why: Its mean distance is close to the astronomical unit the chart is measured in. Its inclination is zero because the ecliptic, the reference plane, is defined by Earth's orbit.
bodies.derived: a_au, perihelion_au, aphelion_au = 10^6 km x 1e6 / au_km (IAU 2012 B2); radius_km = diameter_km / 2

bodies.name: Mars
bodies.why: The outermost rocky planet; beyond it lies the asteroid belt and then the giants.
bodies.derived: a_au, perihelion_au, aphelion_au = 10^6 km x 1e6 / au_km (IAU 2012 B2); radius_km = diameter_km / 2

bodies.name: Jupiter
bodies.why: The largest planet, about eleven Earth diameters across. It takes almost twelve Earth years to go round the Sun once.
bodies.derived: a_au, perihelion_au, aphelion_au = 10^6 km x 1e6 / au_km (IAU 2012 B2); radius_km = diameter_km / 2

bodies.name: Saturn
bodies.why: About twice Jupiter's distance from the Sun; one orbit takes nearly thirty Earth years.
bodies.derived: a_au, perihelion_au, aphelion_au = 10^6 km x 1e6 / au_km (IAU 2012 B2); radius_km = diameter_km / 2

bodies.name: Uranus
bodies.why: An ice giant about twice Saturn's distance; an orbit takes about 84 Earth years.
bodies.derived: a_au, perihelion_au, aphelion_au = 10^6 km x 1e6 / au_km (IAU 2012 B2); radius_km = diameter_km / 2

bodies.name: Neptune
bodies.why: The outermost planet. The Kuiper Belt begins at about its orbit.
bodies.derived: a_au, perihelion_au, aphelion_au = 10^6 km x 1e6 / au_km (IAU 2012 B2); radius_km = diameter_km / 2
